segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So now we we really do have the panorama of all times and moods in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So now that's everything. That's every tense including both the idea of time and the idea of mood.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We've learned how to construct them all and we should really listen actively to refresh any knowledge that we might need to refresh through our exposure to Spanish,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: no? Analyzing always what we hear. And if you're listening to a song or a movie, maybe you just hear the endings of the verbs at the beginning, but if you can identify what that ending means, that's the important bit.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: In the same way, this course has been focused equally on the process that we go through in building our structures in Spanish as it has been focused on content.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So half of the point of this course has been content, has been teaching you Spanish, and the other half has been how to manage Spanish,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: how to manage these elements that we've learned, how to think about this information and how to relate to information generally in a new way, how to find things that you think you might have forgotten.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We've also looked now and then at some irregularities in Spanish,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: verbs or other words that don't follow the rules that we learned.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now the older the language, the more irregularities it tends to have.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Spanish, effectively being modern Latin, is quite prone to irregularities.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But the irregularities can be made sense of within themselves. You can group together irregularities. So whilst throughout the course we were looking at the odd irregularity as it popped up, now at the end of the course, we are going to tidy up the irregular verbs.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So there are a group of verbs which we can call the "-go" verbs.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: These are the verbs that use "-go" instead of "-o" for the "I" form.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, how do you say to have, "to have" for possession?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tener.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tener. And "I have"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tengo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tengo. So this "-go" pops up for the "I" version, but only for the "I" version.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How do you say "he has" or "she has", "you" (formal) "have"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tiene.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tiene. And "you" informal?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tienes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And "they"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tienen.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tienen. And "we"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tenemos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tenemos. So the "-go" is only popping up for the "I" version. What was "to come"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Venir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Venir, good. "I come"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vengo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vengo. So here we have the "-go" again. But "he comes"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Viene.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Viene. "They come"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vienen.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "You" informal?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vienes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "We"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Venemos. Venimos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Venimos, good. So we have this "-go" popping up just for the "I" form. We've seen other verbs like this. What was "to go out" or "to leave"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Salir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Salir. And "I go out" or "I leave"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Salgo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Salgo. "To put"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Poner.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Poner. And "I put"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pongo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Pongo, good. We have decir, "to say" or "to tell", and we get digo, which is even more irregular, but we see the "-go".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We have hacer, "to make" or "to do", and we get hago.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Oír, which means "to hear", oír, and we have oigo, "I hear".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Traer, traer means "to bring" and "I bring" is traigo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So "to bring" is T-R-A-E-R, traer, and then "I" is traigo, it takes an extra "i". So here we get traigo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Traer is interesting because traer means "to bring", but when it forms part of another verb, we can translate it like "-tract".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, extraer means?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Extract.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say "attract"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Atraer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Atraer. "Contract"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Contraer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "Distract"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Distraer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "I distract"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Distraigo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Distraigo, "I distract". Or you could say "I get distracted", me distraigo, good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So these "-go" verbs are a little bit special and they behave quite irregularly, but more or less in the same way.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: One of the things they do in the same way is that in the mood tense, instead of switching vowels like the rest of the verbs do in the mood tense in the present, they go from "-go" to "-ga".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So whilst in the normal present this "-go" only pops up for "I"—we have tengo, tiene, tienes, tienen and tenemos—the "-ga" for the mood tense is for everybody.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we get tenga for "I", "he", "she", "it" and "you" (formal). How would you make it informal?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tengas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly. So if you were to say "I want you to come", "I want that you come" speaking informally, so "I want that"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero que...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Now we want "you come" and we want the mood tense version. So it's a "-go" verb, so our base for the mood tense is venga.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if you want to speak informally and say "I want that you come", "I want you to come"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero que vengas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Quiero que vengas. And you will hear actually in Spain, "¡Venga, venga, venga!" they use it all the time meaning "Come on, come on!" "¡Venga, vale!" they say vale as well in Spain, "¡Venga, vale!" You will hear this all the time when a Spanish person is hanging up the telephone, you can hear 15 of them, "Venga, vale, vale, venga, venga, vale."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this venga that you will hear around a lot will be a nice hook to remember that this "-go" goes to "-ga".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Actually when somebody is answering the phone in Spain, you might hear "Diga" or "Dígame". What does that mean, dígame?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tell me.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. The mood tense by itself is an order. For a positive order then, we have the me after the verb: dígame. So you will hear people answering the phone like this in Spain: "Tell me", dígame.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So traer was "to bring". What is "I bring"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Traigo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Traigo. And what is "you bring", speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Traigas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This is the mood tense, but we don't want the mood tense, we just want "you bring" informally.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Traes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Traes, good. But if you say "I want you to bring it", how would you say that? "I want you to bring it" informally.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero que lo traigas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Quiero que lo traigas. "I don't want you to distract me. I don't want you to distract me", still informal.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No quiero que me distraigas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. No quiero que me distraigas. "I don't want you to distract me." Very good.
